questions.explanation: The line and its residual spread come first, because every later step is a multiple of that spread. Where the target sits relative to the mean of the predictor then matters, since a value far from the mean of the data is harder to predict. The two sources of variation are combined under a square root, the critical value scales the result, and the interval is finally centred on the prediction and described for what it covers.
questions.hint: The residual spread has to exist before any interval can be scaled by it.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the construction of a prediction interval

options.text: Fit the line and obtain the residual standard deviation from the residuals
Take the target value of the predictor and measure how far it sits from the mean
Add the estimation term and the new case's own variation under a square root
Multiply that standard deviation by the critical value for the chosen level
Centre the interval on the predicted value and state what the case represents

questions.explanation: The predictor list and the way each field is measured are settled first, because a field recorded after the outcome it is meant to predict has to be caught while the list is still being written. The data are then split so tuning and measuring use different records, and the model is fitted and tuned on the tuning portion only, without a glance at the held-out records. Measuring once on those records at the end is the only step that produces a number worth reporting.
questions.hint: A predictor recorded after the outcome can only be removed before fitting, not after.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that prevent a data leak

options.text: Fix the list of predictors and the way each one is measured before fitting
Check that no predictor is recorded after the outcome it is meant to predict
Split the data so the records used for tuning are not those used for measuring
Fit and tune on the tuning portion only, never looking at the held-out records
Measure once on the held-out records and report that number as the result

questions.explanation: Patients are grouped by predicted risk first, because a single average probability says nothing about whether the scale is right. The events actually observed in each group are then counted and compared with the average score that group received, and the comparison is only meaningful where enough patients sit. Recalibrating, or retiring the score, is the last step and depends entirely on what those comparisons showed.
questions.hint: You cannot compare a score with reality until the scores have been grouped.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the checks for a calibrated risk score

options.text: Group the patients into bands by their predicted probability
Count the patients in each band and the events that actually occurred there
Compare the observed event rate in each band with the band's average score
Look for a systematic gap, especially in the bands holding the most patients
Recalibrate or retire the score if the gaps are large and consistently signed
